afrobeat.story: In the late 1950s Fela Kuti left Lagos to study at the London School of Music. Back in Lagos he played a mix of highlife and jazz that did not sell. In 1969, on a trip to the United States, he met Sandra Smith, a singer and former Black Panther. She gave him the writings of Martin Luther King Jr., Angela Davis and, above all, Malcolm X. Kuti came to see that he had not been playing African music. He worked it out with drummer Tony Allen. The new music drew on highlife, fuji and jùjú. The name Afrobeat was meant partly to set it apart from the soul of James Brown. Kuti renamed his band Africa '70. It played a residency at his own club, the Afrika Shrine, from 1970 to 1975. Brian Eno and David Byrne carried its polyrhythms into Talking Heads' 1980 album Remain in Light. In the late 1990s and early 2000s Antibalas helped start an Afrobeat scene in Brooklyn. Kuti's sons Femi and Seun play it today.

afrobeats.story: Afrobeats draws on afrobeat, which grew in the 1960s and 1970s and whose groundwork is credited to Fela Kuti and his drummer Tony Allen. Early on, groups such as Trybesmen, Plantashun Boiz and the Remedies mixed American hip-hop and R&B with local melodies. MTV Base Africa launched in 2005, and MI Abaga, Naeto C and Sarkodie were among the first to use it. In 2007 P-Square built their album Game Over on Nigerian rhythms and melodies. In London, DJ Abrantee added an s to afrobeat to present the sound to British dancefloors, and in April 2011 he launched an Afrobeats show on Choice FM. That year Fuse ODG travelled to Ghana, found the Azonto dance, and back in London mixed it with UK funky and grime. D'banj's "Oliver Twist" reached number 9 on the UK Singles Chart in 2012. In 2013 Davido put an instructional dance video for "Skelewu" on YouTube and asked fans to upload their own. In 2014 afroswing grew out of it in the UK, popularised by J Hus. Drake released "One Dance" with Wizkid and Kyla in 2016, and in 2021 Wizkid and Tems became the first Nigerian pop artists on the Billboard Hot 100.

amapiano.story: Amapiano mixes kwaito, deep house, gqom, jazz, soul and lounge music. In the 2000s DJ Spoko, who had moved to Atteridgeville west of Pretoria, DJ Mujava and others made bacardi house, known as sgubhu saPitori. Because amapiano resembles bacardi house, some place its start in Pretoria, but accounts from the Johannesburg townships differ and no single founder is agreed. Kabelo Motha, known as Kabza de Small, moved from eMalahleni to Pretoria and began his music career in 2009. His single "Umshove" came out in 2018, and on 1 October 2019 he released the EP Piano Hub with DJ Maphorisa. The name is the Zulu word for "pianos", and the music is built on piano melodies and log-drum basslines. Kabza de Small credits the producer MDU aka TRP with finding the log-drum sound while trying out new plug-ins. Young people posted dance videos set to it on social media, which fed the dance scene in South Africa. In 2019 it spread across Africa, and in 2022 the online store Beatport gave it its own charts. In 2023 Tyla's "Water" became the first song by a South African soloist to enter the US Billboard Hot 100 in 55 years.

baroque.story: In late Renaissance Florence, a circle of humanists and musicians meeting under Count Giovanni de' Bardi, the Camerata, rejected the many-voiced polyphony of their day and looked to ancient Greek drama. In 1598 Jacopo Peri and the poet Ottavio Rinuccini staged Dafne, sung throughout, and in 1600 Peri's Euridice followed, the earliest surviving opera. Singers were now backed by a basso continuo: a keyboard player read figures written above the bass line and improvised the chords. Claudio Monteverdi, composer of L'Orfeo, auditioned in 1613 for the post of maestro at San Marco in Venice and held it until his death. Trading cities wanted opera houses paid for by subscription, and in 1637 Venice opened San Cassiano, the first public opera house in Europe. Heinrich Schütz took the Venetian style to Germany, and Jean-Baptiste Lully bought patents to be the French king's sole composer of operas. Arcangelo Corelli published concerti grossi that set a full orchestra against a smaller group, and his pupil Antonio Vivaldi wrote hundreds of works on that model. Italian composers moved to the galant style around 1730, while Johann Sebastian Bach kept to the Baroque manner until 1750, and the galant style led into the Classical period.

blues.story: Before the blues, enslaved people in the American South sang field hollers and ring shouts. After emancipation, Black farm workers moved from slavery into sharecropping. In 1903 W.C. Handy first heard the blues at Tutwiler, Mississippi. In 1920 Mamie Smith became the first African American to record a blues song. The women who sang it on the vaudeville stage were led by Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith and Lucille Bogan. In the Mississippi Delta, singers accompanied themselves on slide guitar. Charley Patton and Son House played it before Robert Johnson. In 1923 Sylvester Weaver was the first to record slide guitar, fretting the strings with a knife blade or a bottle neck. Okeh and Paramount began recording African-American music. Blues became a genre of its own as Black families left the countryside for the cities in the 1920s. Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and Willie Dixon, all born in Mississippi, moved to Chicago. In 1948 Muddy Waters's "I Can't Be Satisfied" made Chicago a centre for electric blues. With jazz and gospel, the blues went into rhythm and blues.

bolero.story: The bolero did not come from the Italian opera and canzone then popular in Havana, but from romantic folk poetry sung by a new kind of troubadour in Santiago de Cuba, the trovadores. These itinerant musicians travelled around Oriente province and earned their living by singing and playing the guitar. Pepe Sánchez, born in Santiago de Cuba in 1856, wrote the first bolero, "Tristezas", in 1883. He had no formal training, composed in his head and never wrote his songs down, so most of them are lost. Trovadores who first sang alone with a guitar began to play as duos, trios and quartets. In 1905 the tenor Adolfo Colombo recorded the bolero "La Dorila", through the trovador Sindo Garay, who settled in Havana the next year. Around 1915 the first radio stations spread the bolero in Puerto Rico and Mexico, where Agustín Lara and María Grever wrote boleros of their own. In the 1930s Trío Matamoros mixed it with son into bolero-son, which in the United States became the ballroom rhumba. From the late 1940s, filin singers such as César Portillo de la Luz and José Antonio Méndez turned the bolero toward jazz-influenced crooning.

bossa.story: In the late 1950s the slower samba-canção was the main rhythm in Brazilian music. Samba guitarists had been playing complex chord arrangements since the early 1920s. The nightclubs of Beco das Garrafas, a small dead-end alley in Copacabana, were where it took shape. On Elizeth Cardoso's album Canção do Amor Demais, João Gilberto played guitar on two songs by Tom Jobim and Vinicius de Moraes. Gilberto cut the samba drum band down to one guitar: his thumb played the surdo's part, his fingers the tamborim's. He also sang quietly, where Brazilian singers before him had used brassy, almost operatic voices. His LP Chega de Saudade, released in 1959, fixed bossa nova as a new way of playing samba. Young amateur musicians from Rio's South Zone, such as Carlos Lyra and Nara Leão, joined them. On 21 November 1962 Brazil's consulate presented bossa nova at Carnegie Hall in New York. In 1964 Gilberto, Jobim and Stan Getz released Getz/Gilberto, which won Grammy Awards. In Japan, Sadao Watanabe's 1967 album Jazz & Bossa set off a bossa nova boom. At home, MPB followed; its start is often tied to Elis Regina singing Vinicius de Moraes and Edu Lobo's "Arrastão".

carnatic.story: From the 12th century, Persian and Islamic influence in North India pulled Indian classical music into two styles, and by the 16th and 17th centuries the southern Carnatic style stood apart from Hindustani music. Purandara Dasa (1484–1564) set the graded exercises by which it is still traditionally taught, starting beginners on the raga Mayamalavagowla. In the 18th and 19th centuries its main patrons were the Maratha rulers of Tanjore and the kings of Mysore and Travancore. Three contemporaries, Tyagaraja (1767–1847), Muthuswami Dikshitar (1776–1835) and Syama Sastri (1762–1827), became known as its Trinity. Tyagaraja, whose father worked at the court of Thuljaji, spent most of his life in Thiruvaiyaru and turned down King Serfoji II's invitation to court; about 720 of his songs, in Sanskrit and Telugu, survive. At Fort St. George in Madras, Dikshitar and his brothers heard Western orchestral music and the violin, and his brother Balaswami brought the violin into Carnatic music. Musicians founded the Tyagaraja Aradhana festival at Thiruvaiyaru in 1846, and by the late 19th century Madras had become the music's centre. When the princely states dissolved around independence in 1947, patronage passed to private societies called sabhas that sold tickets to concerts.

cumbia.story: Admiral José Prudencio Padilla wrote that on the night of 18 June 1821 Indigenous people in Arjona greeted the feast of Saint John with gaitas and cumbiambas. In Santa Marta in 1825–26 the Swedish naval lieutenant Carl August Gosselman saw a street dance played on a bamboo flute like a gaita, a maraca and a drum from a fire-hollowed trunk. In Barranquilla in 1888 a woman known as La Cañón set up large cumbiamba circles at the four corners of Bolívar street, danced to drums and flutes. Cumbia had been instrumental; in time, singers were added. Clarinetist Lucho Bermúdez, who grew up in El Carmen de Bolívar, wrote stylized orchestral arrangements of cumbia, and by the 1940s it was spreading from the coast to the rest of Colombia. Record companies on the coast, among them Discos Fuentes, founded in 1934, helped carry it abroad. In 1946 Bermúdez recorded 60 of his compositions for RCA Víctor in Argentina. In Mexico in the 1940s the Colombian singer Luis Carlos Meyer and orchestra director Rafael de Paz made La Cumbia Cienaguera, considered the first cumbia recorded outside Colombia. In 1960s Peru, Los Destellos were among the first to lead cumbia with electric guitars.

dancehall.story: Dancehall began in the late 1970s among working-class people in inner-city Kingston who could not go to dances uptown. As Edward Seaga's government replaced Michael Manley's, music moved away from internationally oriented roots reggae toward local listeners. Radio would not play it, so it spread through sound systems and record dealers. Deejays toasted over rhythm tracks from 1960s and 1970s reggae. Sound systems such as Killimanjaro and Black Scorpio brought new deejays such as General Echo and Yellowman, whose sexually explicit lyrics were called "slackness". Deejay records now mattered more than records by singers. In 1984 Wayne Smith and Noel Davey built a riddim on the "rock" preset of a Casiotone MT-40 keyboard, because Davey could not afford a Yamaha DX-7. King Jammy released it as "Under Mi Sleng Teng" in 1985, and many artists recorded over the same riddim. Afterwards most riddims were made by keyboard players alone. Shabba Ranks won a Grammy for his 1991 album As Raw as Ever, and dancehall's faster electronic beat shaped Reggae en Español.

disco.story: The discothèque came from France: Olivier Coquelin, a French expatriate, opened Le Club in Manhattan on New Year's Eve 1960. In Philadelphia in the early 1970s, the producers Gamble and Huff gave soul lush strings, thumping basslines and sliding hi-hats. On Valentine's Day 1970 the DJ David Mancuso held the first party at his Manhattan home, later called the Loft. Gay men, often harassed in bars, could dance there together without fear of the police. Alex Rosner put the crowd at about sixty percent black and seventy percent gay. Manu Dibango's "Soul Makossa", first released in France in 1972, was taken up by New York's underground disco scene. DJs mixed one record into the next with no break, so the dancing never stopped. Tom Moulton, wanting dance songs to last longer, made the extended mix on the 12-inch record. The films Saturday Night Fever (1977) and Thank God It's Friday (1978) took it into the mainstream. In the United States it declined after Disco Demolition Night on 12 July 1979. It stayed popular in Italy and other European countries through the 1980s. Frankie Knuckles, a disco DJ, went on to help develop house music in the 1980s.

edmpop.story: David Guetta, born and raised in Paris, began as a DJ in Parisian nightclubs and discovered house music on French radio in 1987. Axwell, Steve Angello and Sebastian Ingrosso formed Swedish House Mafia in late 2008 and, with Avicii, took progressive house into the mainstream. From 2009 Guetta scored crossover hits with pop and hip-hop singers: Kelly Rowland on "When Love Takes Over", the Black Eyed Peas on "I Gotta Feeling", Sia on "Titanium". Tim Bergling, born in Stockholm in 1989, taught himself on a pirated copy of FL Studio, and as Avicii had his first Billboard Hot 100 entry with "Levels" in 2011. In the late 2000s the American music industry took up the term EDM to re-brand US rave culture. Mixmag called the result a "drop-heavy, stadium-filling" main stage sound. Avicii and Swedish House Mafia played arenas rather than clubs; in December 2011 Swedish House Mafia became the first electronic act to sell out Madison Square Garden. Avicii's 2013 "Wake Me Up", sung by soul singer Aloe Blacc, drew on bluegrass. The American EDM market began to wane in 2016, and in April that year Guetta and Showtek released a single called "The Death of EDM".

filmi.story: Hindi film song drew on Ramleela, nautanki, tamasha and the Parsi theatre. Its lyrics leaned on Urdu poetry and the ghazal. Ardeshir Irani's Alam Ara (1931), the first Indian sound film, had seven songs. It was shot at Jyoti Studios in Bombay. Its "De De Khuda Ke Naam Pe Pyaare", sung by Wazir Muhammad Khan, is counted as the first song of Hindi cinema. Irani said he had only a pump organ and a tabla player. Singers at first recorded twice, once during the shoot and again in the studio. In 1935 Raichand Boral introduced playback singing to Hindi film in Dhoop Chhaon. Its song "Main Khush Hona Chahun" was sung by a women's chorus led by Parul Ghosh. From 1934 film songs were issued on gramophone records and later played on radio. From 1948 the music director Ghulam Haider trained the singer Lata Mangeshkar. She and her sister Asha Bhosle became two of India's most prolific playback singers. Cheap cassettes carried the songs across Asia and the diaspora until that industry crashed in 2000.

flamenco.story: Romani migrants reached Andalusia in the 15th century and met the Arab-Andalusian music already there. In 1783 King Carlos III issued a decree that improved the legal position of Spain's gitanos. Flamenco took shape at the end of the 18th century in the cities and farm towns of lower Andalusia, and its first written trace comes from Jerez de la Frontera. It was made by three or four dozen gitano families together with Andalusia's urban poor and journeymen. In 1881 the singer Silverio Franconetti opened a flamenco café in Seville where singers competed in public, and out of it came the professional cantaor. Local singers there reworked Andalusian folk songs in their own style, and the paying public's taste pulled technique and themes into one shared form. From 1920 to 1955 promoters staged it in bullrings and theatres as "flamenco opera", and in 1922 Manuel de Falla and Federico García Lorca answered with a cante jondo contest in Granada open only to amateurs. In the flamenco fusion of the 1970s, guitarist Paco de Lucía from Algeciras and singer Camarón de la Isla broke with Antonio Mairena's conservatism, and Paco de Lucía brought in Brazilian music, Arabic music and jazz.

frenchhouse.story: In France in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Cerrone and Sheila and B. Devotion made space disco. In 1987 photographer Jean-Claude Lagrèze ran French Touch parties at the Palace in Paris to introduce house music, with DJs Laurent Garnier and David Guetta. In 1994 Alain Hô (DJ Yellow) and Christophe Le Friant (Bob Sinclar) founded the label Yellow Productions in the Marais. Thomas Bangalter's records for his label Roulé were among the first, and in 1996 Motorbass built house tracks from samples and filtered loops on Pansoul. In 1996 Martin James of Melody Maker used the name French touch reviewing Étienne de Crécy's Super Discount. Daft Punk, Cassius and Air signed to Virgin, and Daft Punk's first album, Homework, made the UK top 10. DJ and producer, separate jobs until then, became one. In 1998 Bangalter, Benjamin Diamond and Alan Braxe, as Stardust, released "Music Sounds Better with You", which sold over two million copies. Around 1998 major labels wanted their releases labelled French Touch, and in 1999 many artists changed course. It returned in the mid-2000s through Justice and Pedro Winter's label Ed Banger, and Madonna drew on it for Confessions on a Dance Floor in 2005.

funk.story: In New Orleans, Dave Bartholomew and Professor Longhair brought Afro-Cuban instruments and the clave pattern into rhythm and blues. Longhair's way with rhythm became a basic template of funk. When Little Richard left secular music in 1957, some of his band joined James Brown and the Famous Flames. By the mid-1960s Brown put the weight on the first beat of every bar instead of the backbeat. The change began with "Out of Sight" in 1964 and "Papa's Got a Brand New Bag" in 1965. In 1990 Brown explained it: "I changed from the upbeat to the downbeat." His arranger Alfred "Pee Wee" Ellis credited drummer Clyde Stubblefield's New Orleans drumming as the basis of modern funk. With "Cold Sweat" (1967), "Mother Popcorn" (1969) and "Sex Machine" (1970), Brown dropped even the twelve-bar blues. In New Orleans the Meters had R&B hits with "Cissy Strut" in 1969. George Clinton's bands Parliament and Funkadelic mixed it with jazz and psychedelic rock. Many early disco songs and performers came straight from funk. From the late 1980s hip-hop artists sampled funk records, and James Brown is said to be hip-hop's most sampled artist.

gagaku.story: From the 5th century, music and dance reached Japan from mainland China and the Korean peninsula; in 554 musicians are said to have come from the Korean kingdom of Baekje. In 701 the Taihō Code set up the Gagaku-ryō, a court bureau for music and dance. In 736 the monk Buttetsu brought Rin'yū music, said to come from India and Southeast Asia; in 752 Tang, Korean and native dances marked the eye-opening of the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji in Nara. In the 9th and 10th centuries the Heian court fused these imported styles with native song, and split the repertoire into a left side built on Tang music and a right side built on Korean music. Courtiers played too: Minamoto no Hiromasa is remembered for the flute and biwa, Fujiwara no Moronaga as a biwa master. After the Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477 the ensembles stopped playing in Kyoto for about 100 years, until the Tokugawa shogunate revived them. After 1868 the guilds of Osaka, Nara and Kyoto moved to Tokyo, where their descendants make up most of the Imperial Palace Music Department. In 1973 Tōru Takemitsu completed Shuteiga (In an Autumn Garden) for the Imperial Household ensemble.

georgianpolyphonic.story: Georgian villagers were singing in parts before Christianity reached Georgia at the start of the 4th century. From the 7th and 8th centuries, Georgian church composers translated Greek Orthodox chants and added harmonies to the single-line melodies. Village singers, mostly farmers, kept the tradition going for centuries. In Kakheti, table songs set two soloists over a long drone bass; in Guria, three or four singers each took a separate line, with a yodel called krimanchuli. As farm work changed, the supra feast became where many kinds of song survived. The first professional choir, formed in 1886, began moving singers toward Western tuning. Under Soviet rule (1921–1991) church songs were forbidden, and huge regional choirs cut back the singers' improvising. In 1968 Anzor Erkomaishvili founded the Rustavi Choir; the Kakhetian song Chakrulo went into space on the Voyager records in 1977, and UNESCO listed Georgian polyphonic singing in 2001.

ghazal.story: The ghazal began as Arabic love poetry in the 7th century, entered Persian in the 10th, and reached the Indian subcontinent in the 12th with the courts of a new Islamic sultanate. In the 13th century Amir Khusrow began writing it in the local Hindavi tongue, putting Persian verse forms into local speech. In the 18th century poets such as Mir Taqi Mir, born in Agra in 1723, moved the ghazal from Persian into Urdu. Poets lived on court patronage, and the state of Oudh paid so well that many moved to Lucknow, Farrukhabad and Faizabad. After Ahmad Shah Abdali sacked Delhi each year from 1748, Mir went to Lucknow in 1782 at the invitation of Asaf-ud-Daulah. In Delhi the Red Fort hosted mushaira gatherings and paid poets such as Ghalib, until the rebellion of 1857 ended that patronage. Akhtari Bai Faizabadi, born in 1914 and later called Begum Akhtar, put ghazals on gramophone records and was among the first women to sing them in public concerts, not private gatherings. In the 20th century she, the Pakistani singer Mehdi Hassan and Jagjit Singh brought Western instruments such as the guitar into the ghazal, and film songs spread it.

gnawa.story: Gnawa music grew from the traditions of West Africans, among them Hausa, Fulani and Bambara people, carried to Morocco by the trans-Saharan slave trade. It took shape in the 16th and 17th centuries, and its songs still keep West African words and speak of abduction, suffering and privation. At the lila, a ritual that runs from late evening until sunrise, a maalem plays the three-string guembri and calls the spirits while his troupe clacks heavy iron qraqeb castanets. The night runs through seven suites, one for each family of spirits, called mluk, each with its own colour, incense, rhythm and dance. Other Moroccan brotherhoods open with their founding saint's Arabic texts; the Gnawa, whose ancestors did not read Arabic, open instead by singing of their enslaved forebears. Since 1998 the Gnaoua World Music Festival in Essaouira has put maalems on stage with Randy Weston, Pharoah Sanders and other jazz musicians. Maalem Mahmoud Guinia, born in 1951, played with Pharoah Sanders and Carlos Santana. In 2019 UNESCO inscribed Gnawa on its list of the intangible heritage of humanity.

gospel.story: Chicago's established Black churches of the time discouraged clapping, stomping and improvising as unrefined. Thomas A. Dorsey moved to Chicago in 1919. From 1923 he led the band accompanying the blues shouter Ma Rainey. At the National Baptist Convention in 1930, Willie Mae Ford Smith sang his song "If You See My Savior". The convention publicly endorsed the music at that meeting, which is why 1930 is often given as the year Black gospel began. With Theodore Frye, music director of Ebenezer Baptist Church, Dorsey trained a new choir to sing his songs with a "gospel blues" sound. With Sallie Martin he set up Dorsey House of Music, the first Black-owned gospel publishing house in the United States. Apart from the words, he saw no real difference between blues and church music. Hundreds of thousands of migrants from the South, used to the blues, were coming to outnumber the church members who preferred European classical music. In 1936 members of Dorsey's junior choir became the Roberta Martin Singers. Sam Cooke of the Soul Stirrers, Ray Charles, Little Richard and James Brown went on to record both gospel and R&B.

gregorian.story: In the fifth century a singing school, the Schola Cantorum, was founded in Rome, while Gaul kept its own Gallican chant and Italy an Old Roman chant. During a visit to Gaul in 752–753 Pope Stephen II said Mass with Roman chant, and Pepin abolished the local Gallican rites in favour of the Roman use, to strengthen ties with Rome. In 785–786, at Charlemagne's request, Pope Adrian I sent a papal sacramentary with Roman chants to the Carolingian court, and a project overseen by Chrodegang of Metz promoted the Roman Mass across Francia. Scholars date this blend of Roman and Gallican chant to around 750; it was fitted into what became the eight church modes. The Metz project also invented neumes, free-form signs showing the shape of a remembered melody. Charlemagne spread the chant through his empire to consolidate religious and secular power, and by the 9th century Gallican chant had effectively been eliminated. The first manuscripts with notation date from around 930, many of them from Regensburg, St. Gall, Laon and St. Martial. Improvised harmonizations of the chant, called organum, opened the way to medieval polyphony, and modern staff notation grew directly from its neumes.

hindustani.story: In the 13th century Sharangadeva wrote the Sangita Ratnakara, whose raga names such as Turushka Todi ("Turkish Todi") show ideas arriving from Islamic culture; it is the last text cited by both the Hindustani and Carnatic traditions. Under the Delhi Sultanate and then the Mughals, musicians found patrons in the new rulers' courts, and Hindu and Muslim ideas met in new forms such as qawwali and khyal. Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi who composed in Persian, Turkish, Arabic and Braj Bhasha, is credited with introducing ragas such as Yaman Kalyan. At Gwalior, Raja Man Singh Tomar (1486–1516) moved classical song from Sanskrit into Hindi, and dhrupad developed at his court. In 1562 Tansen joined the court of the Mughal emperor Akbar, where he introduced new ragas and compositions. When the Mughal Empire broke up, smaller courts such as Oudh, Patiala and Banaras kept paying musicians, and their family styles became the gharanas. In 1901 Vishnu Digambar Paluskar opened the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya school in Lahore, and between 1909 and 1932 Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande sorted the ragas into thaats. Fred Gaisberg's first recordings of Indian music, in 1902, made Gauhar Jan the music's first star.

house.story: After Disco Demolition Night in Chicago, dance music passed from major labels to DJs in the city's underground clubs. Frankie Knuckles, who had moved from New York City, was resident DJ at the Warehouse in Chicago from 1977 to 1982, where the dancers were mainly black gay men. Ron Hardy played at its successor, the Music Box, from 1983. Knuckles mixed songs together instead of playing records one after another, and added a drum machine and a reel-to-reel tape player to make new tracks. By one account, the Importes Etc. record shop labelled his records "As Heard at the Warehouse", shortened to "House". In 1984 Jesse Saunders made "On and On" with a Roland TR-808 drum machine and a TB-303 bass synthesizer. From 1985 more Chicago DJs released their own tracks on newly affordable electronic instruments, for clubs serving mainly black, Mexican American and gay audiences. Phuture's "Acid Tracks" (1987) started acid house. In January 1987 Steve "Silk" Hurley's "Jack Your Body" reached number one in the UK, and Britain had its Second Summer of Love in 1988 and 1989.

japart.story: The koto had been kept to the court, tuned to gagaku, and the shamisen descended from the Chinese sanxian, which reached Japan in the 16th century through the Ryukyu Kingdom and the port of Sakai. Yatsuhashi Kengyo (1614–1685), a blind Kyoto shamisen player, learned the koto from a court musician and first taught it to the public. He replaced the six old koto songs with a new form, kumiuta, and retuned the koto to scales taken from shamisen music. In the Edo period, monks of the Fuke Zen sect, the komuso, walked Japan playing the shakuhachi as meditation and begging for alms, exempt from the shogun's travel limits. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 abolished the shogunate and the Fuke sect, and the shakuhachi was allowed back only to accompany koto and shamisen, later taking the kokyu's place in the trio called sankyoku. Michio Miyagi, born in Kobe in 1894 and blind from the age of eight, joined Western music to the koto, wrote Haru no Umi in 1929 and built a 17-string bass koto. In 1932 the French violinist Renée Chemet arranged its shakuhachi part for violin and recorded it with Miyagi for Japan and Europe.

jazz.story: Jazz grew out of blues, ragtime, spirituals, hymns and marches. Until 1843 Africans in New Orleans danced to drums on Sundays at Congo Square. The brass, drums and reeds of the city's marching and dance bands became the instruments of jazz. Cornetist Buddy Bolden played in New Orleans from 1895 to 1906 and left no recordings. Many early players worked in the bars and brothels of Storyville, the district around Basin Street. Bolden and Jelly Roll Morton were among them. Bolden's band is credited with the "big four", the first syncopated bass drum pattern to break from the on-the-beat march. From 1914 Creole and African-American musicians carried jazz north and west in vaudeville shows. Early in 1917 the Original Dixieland Jass Band made the first jazz recordings. The U.S. government shut Storyville the same year. Louis Armstrong started his career in Storyville. By the time Armstrong joined Fletcher Henderson's band, he was moving jazz toward arrangements and soloists. Henderson and Don Redman developed the "talking to one another" formula for hot swing. Swing big bands then took over the 1930s.

jpop.story: Until the late 1980s, Japanese popular song was sold as kayōkyoku, a name in use since the 1920s. When the singer Hibari Misora died in 1989, many kayōkyoku television shows, among them The Best Ten, were closed. The new name came from J-Wave, a radio station in Roppongi that opened on 1 October 1988 and at first played no Japanese music. Around the turn of 1989 its managing director Hideo Saitō and record-company staff planned to play Japanese records there and chose a "J" to label them. At first the word covered Western-style acts such as Pizzicato Five and Flipper's Guitar. From about 1990 to 1993 the charts were led by acts from the Being agency, among them B'z and Tube, whose songs were sold through tie-ins. From 1994 to 1997 the producer Tetsuya Komuro led dance and techno acts such as TRF and Namie Amuro, with 20 songs that each sold over a million copies. Japan's physical music sales peaked in 1998, and Hikaru Utada's first Japanese album, First Love, released in March 1999, became the best-selling album in Oricon history. In December 2002 the phone company au opened a market for ringtone song downloads.

jungle.story: Jungle grew from the British rave scene and Jamaican sound-system culture as breakbeat hardcore split apart in 1992 and 1993. Shut Up and Dance had put reggae samples into hardcore since 1990. Paul Ibiza of Ibiza Records fused bleeps and breaks with reggae basslines, and Lennie De Ice's "We Are I.E." laid a ragga bassline under the beat. DJs such as DJ Ron, DJ Hype and Fabio & Grooverider played it at clubs such as AWOL and Roast, and on pirate stations such as Kool FM. One account says the name came from a chant, "all the junglists", that Rebel MC sampled in 1991 from a Jamaican sound-system tape. Cheaper sampling let young people make tracks at home, and many producers sampled the "Amen break". It drew black British youths more than other rave styles did. In 1994 and 1995 M-Beat and General Levy's "Incredible" reached the UK top 40, Kiss 100 started a jungle show and BBC Radio 1 followed with One in the Jungle. Dillinja, Roni Size and Krust then moved the sound toward drum and bass, and Roni Size and Reprazent's New Forms won the Mercury Music Prize in 1997.

kpop.story: After the Korean War (1950–1953), Korean singers earned money playing country, blues, jazz and rock and roll for US troops who stayed. The 1980s belonged to ballad singers such as Lee Moon-se and Byun Jin-sub. On 11 April 1992 the trio Seo Taiji and Boys debuted on an MBC talent show with "I Know" and got the jury's lowest rating, but the song and their first album became hits. The song's new jack swing beat and lyrics about the problems of Korean society were followed by hip-hop and R&B acts such as Deux, 1TYM and Drunken Tiger. Their teenage following turned the industry towards teen pop, and in 1995 producer Lee Soo-man, educated in the US, founded SM Entertainment. Agencies took the idol business model of J-pop. Lee's boy band H.O.T. debuted in 1996 after training in singing, dancing, etiquette and handling the media; "Candy" set a formula of energetic dance steps later idol groups adopted. After the 1997 Asian financial crisis H.O.T. released a Mandarin-language album, and the government funded a K-pop department. By the early 2000s TVXQ and BoA succeeded in Japan, and in 2019 South Korea ranked sixth among music markets, led by BTS and Blackpink.

latintrap.story: Latin trap descends from southern hip hop and trap, influenced by reggaeton, R&B and urbano music. Ozuna dates it to "El Pistolón" in 2007, by Arcángel & De la Ghetto, Yaga & Mackie and Jowell & Randy in Puerto Rico; De la Ghetto says he began around 2005 or 2006. Its reggaeton artists wanted to bring American hip hop and R&B to a Spanish-speaking audience. Around 2014 Alvaro Diaz, Myke Towers and Fuete Billete posted songs on social media, and in 2015 and 2016 Noriel, Anuel AA, Bryant Myers and others put trap songs on SoundCloud. In July 2017 The Fader wrote that Puerto Rican rappers had taken trap's lurching bass lines and jittering 808s. They rapped and sang through autotune, in Spanish or Spanglish, about street life, violence, sex and drugs. Jorge Fonseca's compilation Trap Capos: Season 1 was the first Latin trap LP to top Billboard's Latin Rhythm Albums. In 2018 Cardi B's "I Like It", with Bad Bunny and J Balvin, became the first Latin trap song to reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100. In Argentina, Duki, YSY A, Cazzu and others carried it across South America, faster than in Puerto Rico.

mambo.story: In 1910 José Urfé added a montuno, the improvised closing section of the son, to his danzón "El bombín de Barreto". The charanga Arcaño y sus Maravillas, led by the flautist Antonio Arcaño, made popular a danzón with a new rhythm. In the mid-to-late 1930s its players said "vamos a mambear", "let's mambo", of the danzón's final improvisation. Arcaño's cellist Orestes López wrote the first danzón called "Mambo", in 1938. Dámaso Pérez Prado went to Mexico in 1949 looking for work and gave the name mambo to a new style. His band had four to five trumpets and four to five saxophones over bass, drums, congas and bongos. Each phrase ended with a deep sound from the throat. In New York the Palladium Ballroom called itself the "temple of mambo". In Cuba the violinist Enrique Jorrín of Orquesta América is credited with creating the cha-cha-chá. Seeing that dancers had trouble with heavy syncopation, he simplified it. He had the band sing in unison so the words carried. In 1951 he wrote the cha-cha-chá "La engañadora". By the 1970s mambo had been largely absorbed into salsa.

maracatu.story: Maracatu nação grew out of the crowning of Kings of Congo, enslaved people given leadership roles in the enslaved community by the Portuguese administration. Its oldest record, from Pernambuco, dates to 1711. In Recife on 15 November 1800 an enslaved man, Manuel Santiago, broke with Maracatu Brilhante and founded Maracatu Elefante, later the first nation led by a woman. When Brazil abolished slavery in 1888 the Kings of Congo ended, but the nations kept choosing symbolic leaders and staging their coronations. They parade with 80 to 100 drummers on rope-tuned alfaias and a gonguê bell, behind a king and queen dressed as the Portuguese Baroque court. Between the late 19th and early 20th centuries, sugarcane cutters on the plantations of Nazaré da Mata created maracatu rural, also called maracatu de trombone. Around 1991 Chico Science, from Olinda's Rio Doce neighbourhood, co-founded the Mangue Bit movement, and his band Chico Science & Nação Zumbi fused maracatu with rock, funk and hip hop. In the 1990s Maracatu Nação Pernambuco took the genre to overseas audiences, and groups now play it in cities including Lisbon and Toronto.

mariachi.story: Mariachi grew out of the son jalisciense, the string music of the Jalisco area. Its early players used only guitars and harps and dressed in peasant clothes. Most sources place its birth in the town of Cocula, Jalisco, in the 19th century. Gaspar Vargas founded the group later called Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán in the late 1890s. In 1905 a hacienda family brought a mariachi from Cocula to Mexico City to play for President Porfirio Díaz. After the Mexican Revolution the haciendas let their musicians go, and groups wandered and played for a fee, which made them add waltzes and polkas. Farm workers from Jalisco who moved to the capital settled around Plaza Garibaldi. The fashion for jazz and Cuban music brought in the trumpet and pushed the violins back. Tito Guízar was the first film charro to sing mariachi, in Allá en el Rancho Grande in 1936. Silvestre Vargas and his arranger Rubén Fuentes then standardised much of the repertoire. Lola Beltrán and Lucha Villa became the first women mariachi singers. The films also made the music a symbol of ethnic pride for Mexican Americans in the United States.

melodic.story: Kanye West had used Auto-Tune on background vocals for The College Dropout in 2004, but not for lead vocals. In 2008, working on remixes of Lil Wayne's "Lollipop" and Young Jeezy's "Put On", he took to it, and T-Pain coached him. After his mother Donda died in November 2007 and his engagement to Alexis Phifer ended in April 2008, West recorded 808s & Heartbreak in September and October 2008 in Burbank, California and Honolulu. He flew in Kid Cudi, whose 2008 mixtape A Kid Named Cudi he admired, and Cudi co-wrote four songs. West felt rapping could not carry what he felt, so he mostly sang, through Auto-Tune, over the Roland TR-808 drum machine in minor keys. Hip-hop fans and some rappers mocked him for becoming "sappy". Drake's producer Noah "40" Shebib named the album as an influence on the mixtape So Far Gone, released in February 2009 and launched with a party in Toronto. Kid Cudi followed with Man on the Moon: The End of Day in 2009. The album is credited with starting emo rap; B.o.B and Childish Gambino turned to introspection after it, and Juice Wrld and Lil Uzi Vert later named it as an influence.

metal.story: British bands such as the Rolling Stones and the Yardbirds made blues rock by covering blues songs at faster tempos. Cream's first two albums, Fresh Cream (1966) and Disraeli Gears (1967), are counted as models for the style. In 1970 Black Sabbath released Black Sabbath, generally taken as the first heavy metal album. The band's guitarist in Birmingham, Tony Iommi, had lost the ends of two fingers in a work accident. He tuned his guitar down and leaned on power chords, which were easier to finger. The factories and metalworking of Birmingham have also been credited with the band's sound. By 1969 singer Ian Gillan and guitarist Ritchie Blackmore had taken Deep Purple the same way. Judas Priest followed with twin guitars, fast tempos and a sound without the blues. The Sounds writer Geoff Barton named the next wave the New Wave of British Heavy Metal. Its bands, among them Iron Maiden, Saxon and Def Leppard, cut back the blues further and played faster. In the early 1980s bands in the United States built thrash metal from it and hardcore punk.

moderntrap.story: Trap is named after the Atlanta term "trap house", a drug house, and the Atlanta rapper T.I. says he coined the word with his 2003 album Trap Muzik. In the mid-2000s Atlanta producers DJ Toomp, Shawty Redd and Zaytoven set its sound: synth, orchestra and string swells over 808 kick drums. Lex Luger, born in 1991, drummed in church bands, made beats on an unlicensed copy of FL Studio and from late 2008 posted them on Myspace. In 2009 the rapper Waka Flocka Flame wrote back, and later flew him to Atlanta. Luger produced most of Waka's album Flockaveli (5 October 2010): 808 trills, bass kicks, hand claps, dense synthesizers and shifting sub-bass layers under constant ad-libs. He produced more than 200 songs in 2010 and 2011, and other producers copied his sounds. Beats often run in half-time, around 70 BPM, for finer hi-hat subdivisions. The trio Migos, formed in Lawrenceville, Georgia, in 2008, broke out in 2013 with "Versace", produced by Zaytoven. In Chicago, Chief Keef's "I Don't Like" and "Love Sosa" spawned drill as a subgenre of trap. Katy Perry's "Dark Horse" with Juicy J reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 2014.

reggae.story: Reggae grew out of the ska and rocksteady of 1960s Jamaica. Many of its records were built on rocksteady rhythms, slowed enough for a doubled offbeat guitar stroke. The first reggae records came out in early 1968: "Nanny Goat" by Larry Marshall and "No More Heartaches" by the Beltones. That year the Maytals' "Do the Reggay" put the word in print. As record shops spread, producers such as Bunny Lee and Harry J could start out without a sound system or shop of their own. Rastafari shaped the songs: Burning Spear recalled musicians drawing on its emphasis on Africa. In 1968 the Kingston sound-system operator Ruddy Redwood went to Duke Reid's Treasure Isle studio to cut a dub plate. Engineer Byron Smith left the vocal out by accident, and Redwood kept the result. By 1973 these instrumental "versions", made in rival studios, had become dub. That year Lee "Scratch" Perry released Blackboard Jungle Dub, mixed with King Tubby. In South London, singers such as Carroll Thompson and Janet Kay led lovers rock. British reggae in turn fed drum and bass and dubstep.

reggaeton.story: Reggaeton grew out of Panama's Spanish-language reggae of the late 1980s; reggae had reached Panama with Jamaican and Barbadian workers who built the Panama Canal. Its drum pattern was first featured in Shabba Ranks's "Dem Bow" of 1991, and the producers Steely & Clevie are credited with creating it. From 1992 DJ Playero and rappers from around San Juan and Carolina, Puerto Rico, recorded in carports and housing projects such as Villa Kennedy. Their cassettes were sold from car trunks; Daddy Yankee is credited with first saying "reggaeton" on Playero 34. In February 1995 police raided six San Juan record stores and seized hundreds of cassettes under obscenity laws; schools banned baggy clothing and underground music. That year DJ Negro put out The Noise 3 with a label reading "Non-explicit lyrics", and it was a hit. In 2004 reggaeton spread through the United States and Europe, and Daddy Yankee's album Barrio Fino and its single "Gasolina" opened the door for it worldwide. In 2017 the video for "Despacito" by Luis Fonsi featuring Daddy Yankee reached one billion views in less than three months. From 2018, starting with "Te Boté", producers turned to a sharper, minimalist dembow.

rocknroll.story: During and just after the Second World War, fuel shortages and smaller audiences made large jazz bands too costly. Through the late 1940s and early 1950s, R&B players such as Fats Domino and Johnny Otis sped up their tempos. In 1951 the Cleveland disc jockey Alan Freed began playing this music on the radio and calling it "rock and roll". On April 12, 1954, Bill Haley & His Comets recorded "Rock Around the Clock". In July 1954 Elvis Presley recorded "That's All Right" at Sam Phillips' Sun Studio in Memphis. Chuck Berry, drawing on electric blues, made the electric guitar its centrepiece. Independent labels such as Atlantic, Sun and Chess recorded for audiences of their own. It was named and sold as a genre of its own once the industry saw that affluent white teenagers were listening. Haley's song, used in the opening of the film Blackboard Jungle a year after it was recorded, set the boom in motion. As interest faded in America in the late 1950s, groups in British cities such as Liverpool took it up. The Quarrymen, who became the Beatles, moved from skiffle towards rock and roll and rhythm and blues.

romantic.story: In 1810 E. T. A. Hoffmann reviewed Beethoven's Fifth Symphony and set out the principles of musical Romanticism, holding instrumental music to be the art best suited to expressing emotion. Composers had lived under aristocratic patronage; now they increasingly wrote for public concerts with large paying audiences. The move away from Viennese classicism ran through the work of Beethoven and of Franz Schubert, whose Erlkönig is among the first Romantic lieder. In 1821 Carl Maria von Weber's Der Freischütz became the first German Romantic opera. Its centres lay in Berlin, Dresden and Leipzig, where Felix Mendelssohn took over the Gewandhaus Orchestra in 1835 and founded a conservatory in 1843. Better valves and keys from the Industrial Revolution made wind instruments more reliable, and Hector Berlioz enlarged the orchestra. Franz Liszt, a Hungarian piano virtuoso, created the symphonic poem: one movement built on a theme, character or literary text. Richard Wagner took chromatic harmony to its extreme in Tristan und Isolde, and from 1876 the Bayreuth Festival staged only his works. As Romanticism came apart, Arnold Schoenberg and the Second Viennese School answered with Expressionism, and in France Claude Debussy's Pelléas and Mélisande of 1902 carried music towards Impressionism.

rumbacongo.story: It grew from maringa, a Bakongo partner dance of the old Kingdom of Loango, related to West African highlife. In the early 1940s Radio Congo Belge in Léopoldville played records of Cuban son by Sexteto Habanero and Trio Matamoros. In August 1941 Paul Kamba formed the Victoria Brazza band in Poto-Poto. Wendo Kolosoy's "Marie-Louise", written with the guitarist Henri Bowane for the Ngoma label, sold over two million copies. In 1954, 90% of the 30,000 music requests logged by radio were for Congolese rumba. In early 1956 the Loningisa label's session players renamed themselves OK Jazz in honour of their new employer. Congolese musicians moved the piano parts, drum patterns and trumpet phrases of son onto electric guitars and saxophones. Because the imported records were often labelled "rumba", the local music took that name. Antoine Kasongo's orchestra is credited with adding the sebene, a repeated instrumental passage built on guitar figures. In the 1960s and 1970s soukous grew out of it. In the 1980s many musicians left Zaire for Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and Colombia, and for Paris, Brussels and London.

salsa.story: Salsa was built on the son montuno of the Cuban bandleaders Arsenio Rodríguez, Conjunto Chappottín and Roberto Faz. In the 1950s New York danced to mambo played by Machito, Tito Puente and Mongo Santamaría. Its centre, the Palladium Ballroom, closed in 1966 after losing its liquor licence. In the late 1960s the Dominican musician Johnny Pacheco and businessman Jerry Masucci founded Fania Records. Fania brought out Willie Colón, Celia Cruz, Larry Harlow, Ray Barretto, Héctor Lavoe and Ismael Miranda. In 1968 Pacheco formed the Fania All-Stars with Louie Ramírez, Bobby Valentín and Larry Harlow. In 1970s New York the word salsa was first used to sell several styles of Latin dance music. Fania marketed it as one Puerto Rican and pan-Latin sound for people from all of Latin America. In 1971 the Fania All-Stars sold out Yankee Stadium. In the 1980s Colombia, Venezuela, Peru, Mexico and Panama made their own salsa. Its stars included Oscar D'León from Venezuela and Joe Arroyo from Colombia. In Cuba, some say a D'León performance set off the work that became timba.

samba.story: Rio's urban samba drew on rural dance traditions from across Brazil. After slavery was abolished, Black Bahians moved to Rio in growing numbers. Women from Bahia, the "Tias Baianas", founded the city's first Candomblé terreiros. Their homes held cooking and the gatherings called pagodes, where urban samba grew. Regulars at Tia Ciata's house included Sinhô, Pixinguinha, Heitor dos Prazeres, João da Baiana and Donga. "Pelo Telefone", released on 19 January 1917, was a hit at that year's Rio carnival. Donga registered it under his name, and contemporaries said he had taken a collective song. Musicians in the Estácio neighbourhood made a samba with a faster tempo and longer notes. Ismael Silva and his companions marked the beat on the surdo, making the rhythm more syncopated. To avoid police harassment, they organised themselves into what they called samba schools. Their Deixa Falar was the first carnival group to use a bateria of surdo, tamborim and cuíca. Between 1931 and 1940 samba was the most recorded genre in Brazil. Later, a new way of accompanying and singing samba, spread from Rio's South Zone, became known as bossa nova.

ska.story: After the Second World War, Jamaicans bought radios and could hear rhythm and blues from the American South. Ska joined that sound to Jamaican mento and American jazz. To meet the demand, Prince Buster, Coxsone Dodd and Duke Reid set up sound systems. In the second half of 1959 Dodd and Reid began issuing their own recordings of local artists on disc. The first ska records were made at Federal Records, Studio One and WIRL in Kingston. Its rise coincided with Jamaica's independence from Britain in 1962. The producers had turned to recording local artists because new American jump blues and R&B tunes ran short in the late 1950s. Within two or three years the copied American shuffle had become ska, with the guitar chopping on the offbeat. One account credits Prince Buster, who flipped the R&B shuffle beat to stress the offbeats on guitar. Millie Small's "My Boy Lollypop" of 1964 was Jamaica's first international hit. In 1965 and 1966, as American soul grew slower and smoother, ska slowed with it into rocksteady. In the late 1970s, bands around Coventry joined ska rhythms to punk guitar in the 2 Tone style.

son.story: Most musicologists place son's earliest forms in Cuba's Oriente Province. They were made by peasants, many of Bantu origin, unlike the Afro-Cubans of the island's west. Their guitars are thought to have given rise to the tres around 1890 in Baracoa. After slavery was abolished in 1886, many freed people moved into the solares of Havana's poor neighbourhoods. In 1917 the Cuarteto Oriental recorded the first son in the Columbia catalogue. In 1920 it became the Sexteto Habanero. Around 1910 son most likely took the clave rhythm from Havana's rumba. The Habanero's guitar, tres, bongos, claves, maracas and double bass set the line-up of the son sextet. Radio arrived in 1922. Between 1925 and 1928 son moved from the margins to become perhaps Cuba's most popular music. In the late 1920s sextets became septets, with Ignacio Piñeiro's Septeto Nacional among them. In the 1940s Arsenio Rodríguez became son's most influential player. Mambo, from the later 1940s, carried many traits of son. After the Cuban Revolution, son, mambo and rumba fed into salsa, first in New York.

soul.story: Soul grew out of African-American gospel music and rhythm and blues, joining their religious and secular styles in the 1950s. Ray Charles began a run of hits with "I Got a Woman" in 1954. Sam Cooke sang lead in the gospel group the Soul Stirrers before he moved into secular music. In Detroit, Berry Gordy founded Tamla Records, later Motown, on 12 January 1959. He turned a photography studio at 2648 West Grand Boulevard into a recording studio and office. In Memphis, the siblings Estelle and James Stewart ran Stax Records. Stax released hits by Otis Redding, Wilson Pickett and the Staple Singers. Stax put the voice further back in the mix and used horns where other records used backing singers. Motown, an African American-owned label, won white listeners as well. Between 1960 and 1969, 79 Motown songs reached the Billboard top ten. Aretha Franklin, first a gospel singer, began making secular records in 1960 and later recorded for Atlantic. After the 1967 Detroit riot, Gordy moved Motown to Los Angeles. James Brown and Sly and the Family Stone moved on into funk. Neo soul, drawing on hip-hop, grew from it around 1994.

spirituals.story: Spirituals grew from African musical traditions blended with Christian hymns brought by missionaries and slaveholders to enslaved Africans in the American South. The revivals of the First Great Awakening in the 1730s and 1740s converted many enslaved people. The songs first flourished in secret meetings, the hush harbors, and later spread to camp meetings and revivals. They stayed oral until 1867, when the abolitionists Charles Pickard Ware, Lucy McKim Garrison and William Francis Allen printed Slave Songs of the United States, with songs Ware took down from the Gullah people of South Carolina's Port Royal Islands. On 6 October 1871 nine students of the new Fisk school in Nashville, Tennessee, set out as the Fisk Jubilee Singers to raise money for it. At first they left out the slave songs, sacred to their parents; then the Reverend Alexander Reid gave them "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot", learned from Wallace and Minerva Willis, enslaved by the Choctaw. By 1872 they sang at the White House, and in 1873 they toured Europe. Harry Burleigh made spirituals into art songs for solo concert singers. Blues and gospel grew from the spirituals, and civil rights freedom songs such as "Oh, Freedom!" were adapted from them.

swing.story: From 1923 Don Redman's arrangements for the Fletcher Henderson Orchestra set brass and reeds answering each other. In his solos Louis Armstrong accented the second and fourth beats and ran into the main beats with lead-in notes. In the southwest, Black territory bands built dance tunes on riffs played in call and response. In Kansas City, Bennie Moten renamed his signature tune from "Moten Stomp" to "Moten Swing". In 1931 Chick Webb's orchestra began a long stay at the Savoy Ballroom. The Great Depression put Henderson's band out of business in 1934. Henderson then sold arrangements to the bandleader Benny Goodman. At the Palomar Ballroom from 21 August 1935, young white dancers took to Goodman's band. Other dance bands copied him, opening a swing era that lasted until 1946. Dancers answered with the Lindy Hop, which had started in the late 1920s. In 1937 Count Basie's orchestra brought the Kansas City riff style to the Savoy. Small bands led by Louis Jordan and Lucky Millinder played a jump swing that led to rhythm and blues. In 1940 Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and others whom swing had brought to New York began to work out bebop.

tango.story: Tango grew from the payada, the milonga of the Argentine and Uruguayan pampas, and Uruguayan candombe, which had been practised in Argentina since the first enslaved Africans were brought there. The first tango group was two Afro-Argentines, Casimiro Alcorta on violin and Sinforoso on clarinet, who played small concerts in Buenos Aires from the early 1870s to the early 1890s. European immigrants played early tango in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Ángel Villoldo wrote "El Choclo" in 1903 and recorded it himself in Paris, because Argentina had no recording studios. In the 1920s tango moved out of the brothels, and the bandleaders Roberto Firpo and Francisco Canaro dropped the flute and put a double bass in its place. Carlos Gardel helped develop the sung tango canción in the 1920s, and his Spanish-language films for Paramount in the early 1930s fed Argentina's new sound-film industry. In the Golden Age, from about 1935 to 1952, tango was played by orquestas típicas of over a dozen players, among them those of Juan d'Arienzo, Francisco Canaro and Aníbal Troilo. In the 1950s Ástor Piazzolla set out to break tango's classic forms, and he and his followers built nuevo tango from jazz and classical elements.

techno.story: Detroit's high-school parties of the early 1980s danced to European disco, which locals called "progressive", and to synth-pop. The radio shows of The Electrifying Mojo played Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra next to disco and funk. Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson met at Belleville High School, about 30 miles from Detroit, where they were among the few black students. Atkins took the word techno from Alvin Toffler's "techno rebels" when his duo Cybotron, with Richard Davis, released "Alleys of Your Mind" in 1981. The three went to Chicago to hear Ron Hardy and Frankie Knuckles, and joined that dance music to the mechanical sound of Kraftwerk, reflecting post-industrial Detroit. Rejecting the formulas of Motown and R&B, they called their music "post-soul". In 1985 Atkins founded the Metroplex label and released Model 500's "No UFO's"; May's "Strings of Life" followed in 1987. In 1988 the British compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit, compiled by Neil Rushton and May, set techno apart from Chicago house. In the early 1990s clubs such as Tresor opened in empty buildings in former East Berlin, and by 1999 the Love Parade drew a reported 1.5 million people.

teenpop.story: In 1986 ten Swedish disc jockeys, among them Dag Krister Volle, known as Denniz PoP, founded the remix service SweMix. In 1992 Denniz PoP remade a demo by Ace of Base as "All That She Wants". In 1992 Denniz PoP and the nightclub owner Tom Talomaa founded Cheiron Studios in the Kungsholmen district of Stockholm. Denniz took on Karl Martin Sandberg, singer of the funk metal band It's Alive, as a songwriter and renamed him Max Martin. From 1996 Cheiron wrote and produced in a joint venture with Zomba, starting with the Backstreet Boys' debut album. Early in 1998 Jive Records sent the 16-year-old Britney Spears to record "...Baby One More Time", a song first written for TLC, who had turned it down. Cheiron's songs set R&B grooves under Swedish pop melodies with large major-chord choruses, a "happy/sad" quality The Guardian compared to ABBA. Denniz PoP died of cancer on 30 August 1998, aged 35, and Cheiron closed in 2000. In 2001 Martin and Talomaa started Maratone, and Martin went on to work with Kelly Clarkson, Katy Perry and Taylor Swift, writing or co-writing 31 Billboard Hot 100 number ones.

tilawa.story: Islamic tradition holds that Muhammad received his first revelation in 610 in the Cave of Hira, and further revelations over 23 years. The first muezzin was Bilal ibn Rabah, a freed slave of Abyssinian heritage chosen for his loud voice; at the conquest of Mecca in 630 he called the prayer from the Kaaba. In the following generation, reciters in Mecca, Medina, Kufa, Basra and Syria became known as teachers, and their ways of reading took their names. Under the Abbasids, as many non-Arabs became Muslims and mispronunciation spread, scholars began writing down the rules, and Abu Ubaid al-Qasim bin Salam (774–838) was the first to set tajwid in writing. Abu Bakr Ibn Mujahid (859–936) limited the accepted readings to seven. In the adhan each phrase is followed by a longer pause and grows longer and more ornamented on repetition; Medina uses maqam Bayati, Mecca maqam Hijaz. In 1944 Mahmoud Khalil Al-Hussary won Egyptian Radio's reciters' competition, and became the first to record the whole Quran in the measured murattal style. Abdul Basit Abdus-Samad, known for the melodic mujawwad style, joined Egyptian Radio in 1951, and his recitations were broadcast by radio stations in other Arab countries.

tinpan.story: Before it, publishers mostly printed European songs to avoid royalties; only about 10 to 30 percent of music printed in the United States was by American composers. After the Civil War, middle-class families owned pianos and bought sheet music to play new songs at home. From about 1885 publishers gathered in one Manhattan district, and by the late 1890s most had followed Witmark to West 28th Street between Fifth and Sixth Avenues. Many publishers were former salesmen or Jewish immigrants: Leo Feist had sold corsets, Edward B. Marks buttons. Charles K. Harris wrote "After the Ball" in 1892, Irving Berlin "Alexander's Ragtime Band" in 1911. Publishers paid song pluggers, George Gershwin among them, to play new songs in music stores and sell the sheet music. They began with ballads and comic songs, took up the cakewalk and ragtime, later jazz and blues, always in a form amateur singers and small-town bands could play from print. From the 1930s the phonograph, radio and film replaced sheet music as the driving force, and in the 1950s rock and roll, centred on the Brill Building, took over. In 1985 Bob Dylan said he had ended it: "People can record their own songs now."

wadrum.story: Hourglass talking drums are among the oldest instruments of West African griots, traced back to the Bono, the Yoruba, the Ghana Empire and the Hausa. Yoruba tradition names Ayangalu as the first drummer, made a deity at his death, and families whose names begin with Ayan are the hereditary keepers of his craft. The batá drum, dated to roughly 500 years ago, is said to have been introduced by a Yoruba king named Shango, and was played for gods, royalty and ancestors. In a dundun ensemble the leader, the oniyalu, makes the drum talk by copying the three main tones of the Yoruba language. Under the drums an iron bell sounds a seven-stroke key pattern. Drummers sent warnings of attacks and news of ceremonies between villages, which Europeans noticed in the first half of the 18th century. The slave trade brought almost 300,000 Africans to Cuba, where an enslaved Yoruba man named Añabi made the first sacred batá around 1830. In the 20th century the talking drum entered Nigerian jùjú and fuji, and in 1959 Babatunde Olatunji, born in Ajido near Badagry, released Drums of Passion on the Columbia label.

y2krnb.story: On Control (1986), Janet Jackson and producers Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis set funk and disco rhythms in synthesizers and a rap sensibility. In Virginia Beach in 1991, Pharrell Williams and Chad Hugo, entering a talent contest against their friends Missy Elliott and Timbaland & Magoo, were found by producer Teddy Riley. Timbaland, born in Norfolk and schooled in Virginia Beach, went to New York with Elliott when DeVante Swing of Jodeci signed her group Sista. He took hip-hop's drum breaks into R&B, using breakbeats to break up a track's smooth flow. In 1996 he produced most of Aaliyah's One in a Million and Ginuwine's first album, and in 1997 all of Elliott's Supa Dupa Fly. Rodney Jerkins (Darkchild), raised in New Jersey, produced Brandy and Monica's "The Boy Is Mine" in 1998 and Destiny's Child's "Say My Name" in 1999. The Neptunes produced all of Kelis's first album, Kaleidoscope, in 1999 and in 2001 had their first worldwide hit, Britney Spears's "I'm a Slave 4 U". In Britain, bootleg garage remixes, one of them of "The Boy Is Mine", fed the rise of UK garage. In 2004 all 12 Billboard Hot 100 number ones were by African-American artists.
